turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late. The bus never showed and then the wee one kicked off outside, so.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand, sit in. Err, give me a second, this computer's after freezing again.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We were stuck out there an age. She's wrecked, up half the night.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Right. Sorry, say the surname again, it's hopped off the screen... ah leave it. What has you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The itch. Between me fingers and around me waist. It's fierce, worse at night, and I can't sleep with it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The waist, say that bit again. I was half looking at this yoke.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Around me waist, where the elastic sits. And in between the fingers. I'm scratching the skin off nearly. It's doing me head in.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is it going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. About two weeks. Well, actually I can't pin the day, it just sort of crept up.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No, it's three weeks. She was at it before the bank holiday, I mind the Monday.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right so, somewhere between two and three weeks, we'll not row over it. Any fever, were you hot at all with it?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm just tired and cross. Can we move on?
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to creams or tablets? Anything that brought you out in a rash?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you tried on it?

[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Piriton from the chemist, the 4 milligram ones, at night. I stopped them last week, they made me pure dopey. Someone mentioned prednisolone and I never took that. I put a bit of old hydrocortizone on once, did nothing, so I left it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, 4 milligrams or 10? Screen jumped. Say the Piriton again.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Four milligrams, at night, and I stopped it. I already said that.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Hands out for me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeh. Scratch marks between the fingers, and a couple of little burrows. Let's see the waist.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Here, this side. Don't poke it, it's sore.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Papules along the waistband. No pus, not infected. I was going to give you hydrocortisone 1 percent cream, twice a day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hold on. It's not only her. The partner is scratching the same, and the small lad. Nights, mostly.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say that again? The child as well?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes. The little boy and her fella. Both of them itching.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): It's me, himself and the child in the house. And yes they're at it too. I was too tired to start into all that.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, that changes it. Forget the hydrocortisone, I won't be prescribing that. I think this is scabies. Permethrin, the 5 percent cream, Lyclear.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Whole house, the same night. Cool dry skin, neck down to the toes, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the soles of the feet. Leave it on eight to 12 hours, wash it off in the morning, and do the same again in 7 days.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Eight to 12 hours, all of me? And it's permetrin, yeah, not another tablet. I'm not able for more tablets.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cream, not a tablet, and yes even the feet. Hot wash at 60 degrees for the sheets, towels and clothes, and bag anything you can't wash for three days, the same day you put the cream on. The itch can hang on after the mites are dead, so don't go back near the steroid.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll do the washing. She's fit to drop, she won't manage it today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll send the script for the permethrin now. If it's not settled two weeks after the second treatment, come back to me.

spec.situation: Itchy rash between fingers and at the waist, worse at night, partner and child also itch; permethrin cream explained step by step; household treatment and washing advice.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Hydrocortisone 1% cream twice a day was initially considered but then explicitly cancelled after learning other household members were itchy ('Forget the hydrocortisone, I won't be prescribing that').
Household contacts have similar symptoms: partner/husband and the little boy are also itching, mostly at night.
The rash/itching at the waist was described as sore/tender when examined ('Don't poke it, it's sore').
The patient reported being tired/cross in addition to the itch, and caregiver said she had been up half the night and was exhausted.
Prednisolone was specifically mentioned by the patient as something suggested but never taken.
